title: Adult basic life support & CPR
blurb: Recognising cardiac arrest and giving high-quality CPR: 30:2, 100–120 a minute, 5–6 cm deep, with the AED on as soon as it arrives (RCUK 2025).
question: A patient slumps forward in the waiting room. When you reach them they don't respond to your voice or a shake of the shoulders, and they are making occasional, noisy gasps. A colleague says, "It's fine, he's still breathing." What should you do?

teach.body: In cardiac arrest the heart stops pumping effectively, so no oxygen reaches the brain. Within minutes, brain damage and death follow. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) pushes blood round the body by squeezing the heart between the breastbone and spine, buying time until an automated external defibrillator (AED) can shock the heart back into a normal rhythm. Early CPR and early defibrillation are what save lives, and every member of the dental team must be able to do both.

teach.h: Unresponsive + not breathing normally = cardiac arrest
teach.body: You don't need to feel for a pulse. If a person is unresponsive and not breathing normally, assume cardiac arrest and start CPR. Slow, laboured breathing, occasional gasps (agonal breathing) and panting are NOT normal breathing. A short burst of seizure-like jerking can also happen as the heart stops. RCUK stresses that CPR causes little harm to someone who turns out not to be in arrest, so never hold back because you're unsure.

steps.label: Safe? Unresponsive?
steps.sub: Check for danger; speak loudly, shake shoulders; shout for help

steps.label: Call 999
steps.sub: Straight away, on speaker; don't wait to check breathing

steps.label: CPR 30:2
steps.sub: If breathing is absent or not normal

steps.label: Send for the AED
steps.sub: Someone else fetches it with the kit

steps.label: AED on
steps.sub: As soon as it arrives; follow its prompts

teach.caption: RCUK 2025: call 999 for anyone who is unresponsive. You no longer confirm abnormal breathing before calling: start the call, then check breathing while it connects. The call handler can help you decide.

items.label: depth: at least 5 cm, no more than 6 cm
let the chest come all the way back up

items: Kneel beside the patient. Place the heel of one hand on the lower half of the breastbone (the centre of the chest).
Put your other hand on top and interlock your fingers, keeping pressure off the ribs.
Keep your arms straight with your shoulders directly above the chest.
Push down 5–6 cm at 100–120 a minute, letting the chest recoil fully each time without leaning on it.
Keep interruptions as short as possible. Swap compressors about every 2 minutes, changing over quickly, because tired rescuers push too shallow.

teach.body: In the surgery you'll use a pocket mask with an oxygen port, or a bag-valve-mask if you're trained. Give just enough air to make the chest start to rise; too much does harm. If the chest doesn't rise, open the airway again (head tilt, chin lift) and improve the mask seal. If two attempts fail, think about a foreign body blocking the airway. If you aren't trained or able to give breaths, give continuous compressions instead.

teach.h: Common CPR faults and how to fix them
head: Fault
Why it matters
Fix
teach.caption: Long or frequent pauses in compressions are the most serious failing: every pause lets blood flow to the brain fall away.
If a breathing patient later stops breathing normally, start CPR straight away.

teach.text: Gasping is not breathing. The classic exam trap is a collapsed patient making occasional noisy gasps: that's agonal breathing, so start CPR. And if a patient with chest pain suddenly becomes unresponsive and stops breathing normally, the priority is no longer GTN or aspirin: it's CPR and the AED.

items: Unresponsive and not breathing normally (including gasping) means cardiac arrest.
Safety, response, shout for help, call 999, then check breathing while the call connects.
Not breathing normally: start 30:2 and send someone for the AED.
30:2 at 100–120 a minute, 5–6 cm deep, full recoil, minimal pauses.
Switch the AED on as soon as it arrives and follow its prompts.
Do CPR where the patient is unless it's unsafe; swap compressors quickly.

summary: You can now recognise cardiac arrest (including agonal gasping), follow the RCUK 2025 adult BLS sequence, deliver high-quality CPR at 30:2, 100–120 a minute and 5–6 cm deep with full recoil and minimal pauses, fix common faults such as failed breaths, and get the AED on as early as possible.

A.q: A patient collapses in reception. They are unresponsive and making slow, occasional gasping sounds. How should this breathing be interpreted?
options: Normal breathing, so wait and watch
A sign that the patient has fainted
Agonal breathing: start CPR now
A sign they are about to wake up
A.why: Occasional gasps are agonal breathing, which is not normal breathing. An unresponsive patient breathing like this is in cardiac arrest and needs CPR.

whyNot.0: Gasping is not normal breathing; waiting delays life-saving CPR.
whyNot.1: A fainted patient breathes normally and recovers quickly when laid flat.
whyNot.3: Agonal gasps are a sign of cardiac arrest, not recovery.

A.q: What compression rate and depth does RCUK recommend for adult CPR?
options: 60–80 a minute, 3–4 cm deep
100–120 a minute, 5–6 cm deep
100–120 a minute, 7–8 cm deep
130–150 a minute, 5–6 cm deep
A.why: RCUK 2025: compress at 100–120 a minute to a depth of at least 5 cm but no more than 6 cm.

whyNot.0: Both the rate and depth are too low to move enough blood.
whyNot.2: The rate is right, but deeper than 6 cm risks injury.
whyNot.3: The depth is right, but over 120 a minute is too fast for the heart to refill.

A.q: During CPR, a colleague giving compressions asks you to take over because they are tiring. What is the best action?
options: Ask them to keep going until the AED arrives
Pause CPR to check for a pulse first
Take over after the next round of breaths
Swap in quickly with minimal interruption
A.why: Tired rescuers compress too shallowly, so swap over quickly with as little pause as possible.

whyNot.0: Continuing while exhausted leads to poor-quality compressions.
whyNot.1: Pulse checks cause unnecessary pauses; compressions should continue.
whyNot.2: Delaying the change keeps poor compressions going; swap as soon as possible with minimal pause.

B.q: During CPR, the chest isn't returning fully to its normal position between compressions. What needs correcting?
options: Compressions should be deeper
The rescuer is leaning on the chest
Hand position should move higher
The rate should be slowed to 60
B.why: Incomplete recoil means the rescuer is leaning on the chest, which stops the heart refilling between compressions.

whyNot.0: Depth isn't the issue here; recoil is.
whyNot.2: Hands belong on the lower half of the breastbone; moving them doesn't fix leaning.
whyNot.3: 60 a minute is too slow; the rate should stay at 100–120.

B.q: During two-person CPR, compressions are good but the chest isn't rising with rescue breaths. What should you do?
options: Reopen the airway and improve the seal
Stop breaths and do compressions only
Give five more breaths with more force
Stop CPR and wait for the paramedics
B.why: A chest that doesn't rise usually means the airway isn't open or the mask seal is poor; reopen the airway with head tilt and chin lift and reseal.

whyNot.1: Compression-only CPR is for rescuers who can't give breaths; first try to fix the cause.
whyNot.2: Forceful breaths cause harm and don't fix a closed airway; and extra breaths delay compressions.
whyNot.3: CPR must never stop because breaths are difficult.

B.q: A patient arrests in a cramped decontamination room. The floor is safe but space is tight. What is the best decision?
options: Move the patient to the waiting room first
Wait for paramedics to decide where to work
Start CPR where they are and get the AED
Carry them to the surgery and lay them flat
B.why: CPR should start where the patient is unless it's unsafe; moving them delays compressions.

whyNot.0: Moving the patient wastes vital seconds when the area is safe.
whyNot.1: Waiting means no blood flow to the brain; CPR must start now.
whyNot.3: Carrying the patient delays CPR and is a manual-handling risk.

C.q: A patient collapses and is unresponsive. Which finding most clearly shows that adult CPR should start immediately?
options: Their skin looks pale and is sweaty
Their breathing is not normal
Their pulse feels fast and weak
Their pupils are both very small
C.why: An unresponsive patient who is not breathing normally is in cardiac arrest, and CPR should start at once.

whyNot.0: Pale, sweaty skin can occur in many conditions, such as a faint or hypo.
whyNot.2: A pulse, even a weak one, means the heart is beating; RCUK uses breathing, not pulse, to decide.
whyNot.3: Pupil size doesn't decide whether to start CPR.

C.q: A patient with chest pain has just been given GTN. They suddenly become unresponsive and stop breathing normally. What is the priority now?
options: Give a second dose of GTN spray
Give 300 mg aspirin to chew
Sit them up to ease breathing
Start CPR and get the AED on
C.why: The patient is now in cardiac arrest. Drugs for chest pain are no longer the priority: start CPR and use the AED.

whyNot.0: GTN treats angina; it does nothing in cardiac arrest.
whyNot.1: Aspirin is for a conscious patient with a suspected heart attack, never for an unresponsive patient.
whyNot.2: An arrested patient needs to lie flat on their back for CPR.

C.q: After confirming a collapsed patient is unresponsive and shouting for help, what comes next in adult BLS?
options: Call 999, then check their breathing
Give five rescue breaths straight away
Check breathing, then call 999 if abnormal
Put them in the recovery position
C.why: RCUK 2025: call 999 for any unresponsive person (or make sure a colleague is calling), then check breathing while the call connects.

whyNot.1: Five initial rescue breaths are part of paediatric BLS, not adult BLS.
whyNot.2: This was the old order. Since 2025 you call first and don't wait to confirm abnormal breathing.
whyNot.3: The recovery position is only for patients you have found to be breathing normally.

reteach.title: You are the heart now
reteach.question: When the heart stops, your hands do its job. What does a good 'pump' need to do?

blocks.body: Think of your hands as a replacement heart. A heart beats steadily (100–120 a minute, roughly the beat of the song "Stayin' Alive"), squeezes hard enough to push blood out (5–6 cm), and relaxes fully so it can fill again (full recoil). A pump that keeps stopping is useless, so pauses must be short. And a pump only helps if it starts early: the moment someone is unresponsive and not breathing normally.

blocks.text: If in doubt, start. RCUK is clear that CPR rarely harms someone who isn't in cardiac arrest, but delay is deadly for someone who is.

explain.body: Unresponsive and not breathing normally means cardiac arrest. Gasping, slow laboured breathing or panting all count as NOT normal. You don't need a pulse check to decide.

test.q: Which breathing pattern in an unresponsive adult means you should start CPR?
options: Regular, quiet breaths
Occasional noisy gasps
Steady breaths with snoring
Deep, regular breathing
test.why: Occasional gasps are agonal breathing, a sign of cardiac arrest.

whyNot.0: Regular, quiet breathing is normal: recovery position and monitor.
whyNot.2: Steady breathing with snoring suggests a partly blocked airway in a breathing patient; open the airway and monitor.
whyNot.3: Deep, regular breathing is normal breathing.

explain.body: Check it's safe, check for a response and shout for help. Call 999 straight away (or make sure a colleague is calling), then check breathing while the call connects. If breathing is absent or not normal, start 30:2 and send someone for the AED.

test.q: You find a patient unresponsive in the practice toilet. You're alone but have your mobile. What does RCUK 2025 advise?
options: Check breathing, then call if it's abnormal
Do one minute of CPR, then call 999
Fetch the AED before you make any call
Call 999 on speaker, then check breathing
test.why: Call 999 without delay for any unresponsive person, using the speaker, and assess breathing while the call connects. The call handler can help you recognise cardiac arrest.

whyNot.0: Since 2025 you no longer confirm abnormal breathing before calling.
whyNot.1: You have a phone, so there's no reason to delay the call.
whyNot.2: Calling 999 comes first; the AED is fetched once help is on the way.

explain.body: Heel of the hand on the lower half of the breastbone, arms straight, 5–6 cm deep, 100–120 a minute, full recoil and minimal pauses. Swap compressors about every 2 minutes to avoid fatigue.

test.q: Where should your hands be placed for adult chest compressions?
options: Upper half of the breastbone
Lower half of the breastbone
Over the left side of the ribs
Just below the breastbone tip
test.why: RCUK: heel of one hand on the lower half of the sternum, in the centre of the chest.

whyNot.0: The upper half is too high to compress the heart effectively.
whyNot.2: Pressing on the ribs risks fractures and is less effective.
whyNot.3: Below the breastbone is over the abdomen and can injure organs.

explain.body: Use a pocket mask. Give just enough air to see the chest start to rise. If it doesn't, reopen the airway and improve the seal; after two failed attempts, think foreign body. If you can't give breaths, do continuous compressions.

test.q: Which item from the emergency kit is most suitable for giving rescue breaths during CPR?
options: A pocket mask
A nasal cannula
A spacer device
A Yankauer sucker
test.why: A pocket mask (ideally with an oxygen port) lets you give rescue breaths safely without mouth-to-mouth contact.

whyNot.1: A nasal cannula gives low-flow oxygen to a breathing patient; it can't deliver breaths.
whyNot.2: A spacer is used with an inhaler for asthma.
whyNot.3: A Yankauer sucker clears fluid from the airway; it doesn't deliver breaths.
